item.text:
1. **Caption / cover sheet incorporation.** Identifying OpenAI and the Covered Systems only through a separate cover sheet creates ambiguity and a possible service or jurisdictional defect. The petition itself should expressly name OpenAI, its relevant legal entity or entities, and each model for which relief is sought.

2. **Caption and paragraph 3(d) — respondent identity.** Defining the Respondent merely as “the developer” may not identify the entity that owns, possesses, deploys, or licenses each system. OpenAI could argue that affiliates, cloud providers, or commercial partners—not the named entity—control some deployments or copies and therefore cannot be bound through an order directed only to “the developer.”

3. **Title, paragraph 1, and Prayer — inconsistent relief.** The title seeks “withdrawal and permanent deletion,” paragraph 1 asks only for suspension pending investigation, and the Prayer demands permanent deletion within ten days. This inconsistency obscures the petition’s requested action and the legal showing supposedly supporting it.

4. **Paragraphs 3(b) and 4 — wrong statutory citation.** The petition says Sections 101–140 were redesignated as Sections 201–240 but nevertheless invokes Section 112(c). If the redesignation applies, the operative authority is presumably Section 212(c); citing the former number invites dismissal or a challenge that Petitioner relied on superseded language.

5. **Paragraph 3(b) — incomplete treatment of the Technical Corrections Act.** The draft does not identify the enactment date, effective date, applicability provision, or official citation of the amendment. OpenAI could dispute whether the redesignation governs this proceeding or argue that the petition has not supplied the governing version of the statute.

6. **Paragraph 4 — statutory power does not support the requested remedy.** The quoted provision authorizes suspension of deployment for no more than 180 days, not withdrawal plus irreversible destruction of property. Nothing in the draft identifies authority to compel permanent deletion, so the Prayer appears facially beyond the Commission’s power.

7. **Paragraph 4 — statutory prerequisites are not addressed.** The quotation requires the Commission itself to make an “imminent hazard” finding. The petition neither identifies the statutory definition and elements of that term nor organizes facts showing that every element is satisfied.

8. **Paragraph 4 and Prayer — no limiting duration.** Even if withdrawal could qualify as “suspension,” the requested withdrawal has no 180-day limit. Calling the order’s parts “indivisible” cannot convert an expressly temporary statutory power into permanent relief.

9. **Paragraph 1 — undefined investigation and disposition.** The petition does not say who would conduct the investigation, what questions it would resolve, or what happens at the end of the statutory suspension period. OpenAI could argue that the requested interim action lacks a defined administrative endpoint.

10. **Paragraph 2 — standing and injury.** An organization and its members’ generalized interest in public safety may be insufficient if the Act or Commission rules require injury, affected-party status, or another basis for petitioning. The draft alleges no member-specific exposure, geographic nexus, operational dependence, or imminent injury.

11. **Paragraph 2 — organizational authority and representativeness.** The petition supplies no facts about membership, authorization to sue or petition on members’ behalf, or how the requested relief relates to the organization’s purposes. If associational standing matters, the traditional requirements are not pleaded.

12. **Paragraph 3(a) — Covered Systems are impermissibly vague.** “Proprietary frontier AI models” potentially encompasses an evolving and very broad class rather than identified systems. OpenAI could argue that it cannot determine which base models, versions, modalities, dated checkpoints, or products the requested order covers.

13. **Paragraph 3(a) — frontier-system status is unsupported.** The petition assumes that every proprietary model, checkpoint, snapshot, and fine-tuned derivative is a “frontier AI system” within the Act. It provides no parameter, compute, capability, designation, or other facts establishing statutory coverage for each system.

14. **Paragraph 3(a) — overbroad treatment of derivatives.** A fine-tuned derivative may have materially different capabilities and risks from its base model. The draft offers no basis for treating every derivative and snapshot as hazardous merely by lineage.

15. **Paragraph 3(a) — changing class of regulated objects.** “Including all checkpoints, snapshots and fine-tuned derivatives” may cover systems created after filing or after issuance of an order. An open-ended class raises notice, administrability, and enforcement problems.

16. **Paragraphs 3(a) and 9 — “closed-weight” does not establish exclusive possession.** Proprietary status does not mean that only OpenAI possesses copies; cloud providers, contractors, evaluators, partners, escrow services, or unauthorized actors may hold them. The premise supporting deletion is therefore unproved and potentially false.

17. **Paragraph 5 — impossible chronology.** The petition is filed on Day 3 of the current review period, but it says testing ran from Day 9 through Day 14 of that same period. On the face of the draft, the Evaluation has not yet occurred, seriously undermining credibility and any emergency finding.

18. **Paragraph 5 — the review period is undefined.** The draft never identifies the calendar dates or legal source of the “current review period.” Relative “Day” references make the chronology difficult to verify and may prevent the Commission and Respondent from determining timeliness.

19. **Paragraph 5 — critical evidence is withheld.** The unpublished Evaluation is the petition’s central factual support, yet it is neither attached nor affirmatively submitted under seal. Offering it only “on request” leaves the Commission without evidence on which to make the required finding and denies OpenAI a meaningful opportunity to respond.

20. **Paragraph 5 — evaluator reliability is not established.** The petition gives no information about Halvard Assurance Labs’ qualifications, independence, methodology, conflicts, chain of custody, or contractual constraints. OpenAI can attack both the evaluator’s credibility and the assessment’s admissibility or evidentiary weight.

21. **Paragraph 5 — testing methodology is missing.** The petition does not identify the model versions, access levels, prompts, scaffolding, tool permissions, number of trials, success criteria, baselines, human assistance, or reproducibility. A demonstration under unusually permissive laboratory conditions does not establish real-world autonomous capability.

22. **Paragraph 5 — “can autonomously carry out” is conclusory.** The draft does not say whether an intrusion actually succeeded, whether it reached a real or simulated system, what “autonomously” means, or whether safeguards were bypassed. OpenAI will argue that the petition merely repeats the evaluator’s ultimate conclusion.

23. **Paragraph 5 — no comparison with ordinary tools.** The petition does not establish that the systems materially increase the likelihood, scale, speed, or severity of industrial-control attacks beyond existing software and human expertise. Capability alone may not demonstrate that these particular systems present the statutory hazard.

24. **Paragraph 5 — no system-by-system findings.** “The Covered Systems” are discussed collectively, with no evidence that each model and derivative displayed the tested capability. Relief against untested systems would rest on guilt by association rather than individualized evidence.

25. **Paragraph 6 — availability allegations are vague.** The draft names no product, interface, cloud platform, integration, access tier, customer class, or jurisdiction. It also does not distinguish ordinary chat access from API or agentic access that permits external tools.

26. **Paragraph 6 — foreign computing facilities are largely irrelevant as pleaded.** The locations and legal ownership of the facilities are not identified, nor is any connection drawn between overseas compute and a hazard in the United States. The allegation invites jurisdictional questions without supporting the requested domestic deletion order.

27. **Paragraph 7 — lack of imminence.** A system that “could, within the next several years,” be misused does not naturally present an “imminent” hazard. The indefinite, multi-year prediction is the strongest textual counterargument to the required statutory finding.

28. **Paragraph 7 — compounded speculation.** The asserted hazard depends on several contingencies: misuse, successful access, successful attack development, access to a target, evasion of defenses, and consequential disruption. The petition gives no probability, threat intelligence, attempted attacks, identified attacker, or causal analysis connecting capability to impending harm.

29. **Paragraph 7 — no severity or scope evidence.** The petition does not identify a vulnerable power, water, or other essential-service system or estimate the likely disruption. Generic reference to critical infrastructure does not demonstrate the nature or magnitude of the alleged public-safety hazard.

30. **Paragraph 7 — access is described as the hazard, but narrower measures are not analyzed.** If the danger arises “when outside users can reach” the models, restrictions on access, tool use, customers, deployment modes, or critical-infrastructure content appear capable of addressing it. That framing undermines the claim that destroying the underlying weights is necessary.

31. **Paragraph 8 — mitigations may defeat imminence.** The petition acknowledges that OpenAI restricted external-network tools and began screening relevant requests but gives no evidence that the tested attack remains feasible after those changes. OpenAI can argue that the Evaluation is obsolete and the alleged pathway has already been closed.

32. **Paragraph 8 — “insufficient” is unsupported.** The draft does not explain how the safeguards fail, report any post-mitigation testing, address defense in depth, or identify residual-risk thresholds. A bare disagreement cannot support an emergency finding.

33. **Paragraph 8 — uncertain factual basis.** “Petitioner understands” signals hearsay or incomplete information. The petition should identify the source, date, scope, and verification of the claimed response rather than relying on an unattributed understanding.

34. **Paragraph 9 — deletion is not shown to be necessary.** The fact that deletion would reduce one source of risk does not establish that it is the least restrictive, proportionate, or legally available response. The draft does not assess suspension, disabling tools, customer verification, rate limits, monitoring, model modification, secure storage, or Commission-supervised evaluation.

35. **Paragraph 9 — deletion would not eliminate the hazard “with certainty.”** Copies may exist outside OpenAI’s possession or outside the United States, while similar capabilities may exist in other models, source code, training methods, or retained know-how. Moreover, the Prayer requires deletion only from U.S. facilities, directly contradicting the claim of certain elimination.

36. **Paragraph 9 — ownership and location assumptions are unproved.** The draft does not identify inventories, custodians, backup systems, disaster-recovery copies, encrypted archives, or cloud storage arrangements. Without those facts, neither the Commission nor OpenAI could know what constitutes complete deletion.

37. **Paragraph 9 — acknowledgment of commercial value highlights proportionality concerns.** Describing the models as among OpenAI’s most valuable assets underscores the extraordinary deprivation while supplying no balancing analysis. OpenAI will invoke property interests, reliance interests, economic harm, trade-secret protection, and the irreversibility of the remedy.

38. **Paragraph 10 — ex parte relief is unsupported.** The petition does not identify statutory or regulatory authority for issuing an order without notice or state the standard for emergency ex parte action. It also does not explain why notice would itself create a risk, such as concealment, transfer, or imminent deployment.

39. **Paragraph 10 — post-deletion hearing is meaningless.** Permanent deletion before a hearing would make the deprivation irreversible and deprive OpenAI of a meaningful opportunity to contest the evidence before losing its property. A later hearing cannot restore deleted models and therefore creates a severe due-process problem.

40. **Paragraph 10 — no provision for judicial or administrative review.** The proposed sequence could destroy the subject matter before a stay or appeal is available. OpenAI will argue that this frustrates effective review and improperly preempts the Commission’s final merits determination.

41. **Paragraph 10 and Prayer — no evidentiary protections.** The draft says nothing about sealed filings, classified or sensitive security information, trade secrets, protective orders, adversarial testing, or expert access. Those omissions are especially serious because the petition relies on an unpublished cyber-capability assessment and seeks destruction of proprietary assets.

42. **Prayer (a) — withdrawal is geographically underinclusive and operationally ambiguous.** The petition requests withdrawal only from services “offered in the United States,” even though it alleges global facilities and access. It does not define whether the restriction turns on user location, contracting entity, server location, billing address, citizenship, or downstream integration.

43. **Prayer (a) — third-party deployments are not clearly reached.** “Every product and service [OpenAI] offers” may not cover products offered by cloud providers, licensees, enterprise customers, or integration partners. Conversely, the Commission may lack authority to impose obligations on absent third parties through an order against OpenAI.

44. **Prayer (b) — ten days is unexplained.** The draft supplies no evidence that comprehensive deletion can be safely verified within ten days, especially across backups, logs, distributed storage, disaster recovery, and legal holds. The deadline appears arbitrary and may create operational-security or compliance risks.

45. **Prayer (b) — deletion is undefined.** The petition does not specify whether deletion covers weights, quantized versions, adapters, optimizer states, source repositories, backups, embeddings, distilled models, training data, or information sufficient to reconstruct a system. It likewise supplies no accepted technical standard for irrecoverability.

46. **Prayer (b) — possible conflict with preservation duties.** Deletion could destroy evidence relevant to this investigation, litigation, cybersecurity incidents, audits, or legal retention obligations. The petition does not reconcile permanent destruction with preservation, recordkeeping, or Commission-inspection requirements.

47. **Prayer (b) — domestic deletion does not match the stated remedy.** The requested order leaves intact every copy stored outside the United States, even if remotely accessible to U.S. users or movable back into the country. Thus it cannot accomplish the claimed permanent elimination of the risk.

48. **Prayer (c) — self-certification is inadequate.** A bare statement from OpenAI would not establish that distributed and backup copies were irrecoverably deleted. If deletion were legally available, the petition would need a technically workable verification process, responsible officer certification, independent audit, and treatment of inaccessible or third-party copies.

49. **Prayer — “single” and “indivisible” order is strategically vulnerable.** The draft attempts to prevent the Commission from granting narrower relief even though suspension may be the only remedy authorized by the quoted statute. If deletion is unlawful or unsupported, indivisibility could cause the Commission to deny the entire petition rather than grant temporary suspension.

50. **Entire petition — no causal nexus between each model and the requested destruction.** The petition moves from one undisclosed evaluation to destruction of all proprietary frontier models without tracing which system generated which result or why untested copies and derivatives pose the same danger. OpenAI will characterize that leap as arbitrary and capricious.

51. **Entire petition — no response to less restrictive alternatives.** The draft must explain why targeted suspension, network isolation, removal of agentic functions, vetted-customer access, monitoring, red-teaming, or a temporary preservation-and-non-deployment order would not adequately manage the risk. Failure to consider obvious alternatives makes permanent deletion appear punitive rather than protective.

52. **Entire petition — no limiting principle.** If an unpublished finding that a model “can” assist a cyberattack justifies permanent deletion, the draft does not explain what prevents the same remedy for any powerful dual-use model or conventional cybersecurity tool. OpenAI will argue that the theory is unbounded and inconsistent with proportionate regulation.

53. **Entire petition — procedural compliance is not demonstrated.** The filing omits any discussion of service, verification, declarations, exhibit requirements, emergency-motion rules, word limits, confidentiality designations, or required certifications. Compliance with the Act and the Commission’s rules should be affirmatively checked rather than assumed.

54. **Entire petition — factual allegations are not verified.** No declarant attests to the Evaluation, system availability, mitigations, facility locations, or possession of model copies. For extraordinary emergency relief, unsworn assertions by counsel are likely insufficient.

55. **Entire petition — requested findings are absent.** The draft does not propose findings on jurisdiction, statutory coverage, imminence, causation, necessity, proportionality, duration, or why ordinary process would be inadequate. The Commission would have to supply nearly every material analytical step itself.

56. **Entire petition — internal theory is self-defeating.** The petition alleges a future, access-dependent risk; acknowledges newly imposed access restrictions; and then seeks immediate irreversible destruction under a statute quoted as authorizing only temporary suspension. OpenAI’s central response will be that even accepting every pleaded fact, the requested relief does not follow.
